Welcome toThe Legendre Transform

A convex curve, a tangent and its intercept — follow them as the slope changes.

About: labelling the points of a convex curve by the slope of the tangent

Source

Concept
The Legendre transform g(s) = f − sx of the parabola f(x) = ½k(x − a)² + f₀ with k fixed at 0.5, set beside h(s), the height of the curve at the point where the slope is s. All quantities are pure numbers, with no units.
Serves
Explaining which way of labelling a convex curve by slope keeps enough information to rebuild the curve: the operation that turns the internal energy U(S, V) into the Helmholtz function F = U − TS.
Inquiry
Five questions: the intercept as the tangent point moves; the slope of the g(s) trace; a sideways shift a; a vertical shift f₀; rebuilding from tangent lines. A closing card links g = f − sx to F = U − TS.
Misconception
The common wrong ideas are carried by the answer choices; each explanation appears only after a choice is made.
On screen
Left: the curve on fixed axes (x from −2 to 4, height from −3 to 5), the tangent point with its dashed drop, the tangent line Y = f + s(X − x) and its intercept g on the vertical axis. Right: g(s) in blue and h(s) in orange against s, on the same vertical scale; after a change of a or f₀ the previous traces stay as faint dashed curves (one previous setting). The Readouts panel below the controls: x, s, f, g, h and dg/ds; dg/ds is the slope of the blue trace from neighbouring values of g and s at x ± 0.001.
Controls
Drag the tangent point along the curve, or use the x slider or its number box (−1.50 to 3.00); the sweep runs x from −1.50 to 3.00 in 4 s; a moves the curve sideways, f₀ moves it up and down; the rebuild switch hides the curve, its dot and its drop, and draws 31 lines Y = g + sX from slopes and intercepts read off the blue trace.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honours it
Commit, then checkEach question is answered by choosing an option before its explanation appears; the sim stays fully usable throughout.
Readouts only when usedWhile a question is open the Readouts panel shows only the two numbers that question uses; all six appear in free exploration.
Before and after, side by sideChanging a or f₀ keeps the previous traces as faint dashed copies, so new traces can be laid against old ones.
Stable scalesBoth charts use fixed axes with the same vertical scale, so a height on the plot lines up with the same height on the chart and every shift stays visible.
Operational quantitiesdg/ds is measured from neighbouring values of g and s, never typed in as a formula; rebuilt lines use only (s, g) pairs read from the trace.
Formal layer on demandThe equations live in The Physics sheet, opened from the top bar.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Where the intercept goes

Keep a = 0 and f₀ = 0.50. Move the tangent point slowly from x = 0 to x = 3.00 (drag the dot, or type x in the box), watching the blue dot on the vertical axis. What does the intercept g do?

2 · The slope of the blue trace

Set x = 2.00 with a = 0 and f₀ = 0.50, and press Sweep to trace g(s) in the right-hand chart. Then set the tangent point to a few other values of x and compare the dg/ds readout with x. What is the slope of the blue trace?

3 · Shifting the curve sideways

With a = 0 and f₀ = 0.50, press Sweep. Then set a = 1.0, which moves the curve one unit to the right, and press Sweep again. Compare the new traces with the dashed copies of the old ones. What happens to the two traces?

4 · Shifting the curve up

Keep a = 0 and set x = 2.00, where s = 1.00. Raise f₀ from 0.50 to 1.00, watching h and g in Readouts, then press Sweep to redraw the traces. What happens to h and g?

5 · Rebuilding the curve

Set a = 1.0 and f₀ = 0.50, press Sweep, then turn Rebuild from tangents on. The curve is hidden; each line drawn uses only a slope s and its intercept g read from the blue trace. What do the lines outline?

6 · What this shows

Labelling a convex curve by its slope s keeps all the information only if the label is the intercept, g(s) = f − sx. The tangent point comes back as x = −dg/ds, and the tangents rebuild the curve. The height at slope, h(s), forgets sideways shifts.

This is the step from U(S, V) to the Helmholtz function F = U − TS: the slope is T = ∂U/∂S, and S = −∂F/∂T comes back out.

A Curve Labelled by Its Slope

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A convex curve can be labelled point by point by its slope instead of its position. This sim draws f(x) = ½k(x − a)² + f0 with a tangent you move along it, and traces two ways of labelling the curve by slope, g(s) and h(s); the same exchange turns U(S, V) into F = U − TS.

What you'll learn

  • How the tangent's intercept g is built from the point x and the slope s.
  • How g and the height at slope h respond as the tangent point moves.
  • How each responds to a sideways shift a and a vertical shift f0.
  • What it takes to rebuild the curve from its labels.
The sim's opening state: the tangent at x = 2 has slope s and meets the vertical axis at g.

What's on screen

  • White curve (left): f(x), with a white dot at the tangent point and a dashed drop to the x axis.
  • Blue line and dot (left): the tangent, with slope s, and its intercept g on the vertical axis. On the right, the blue trace is g(s).
  • Orange trace (right): h(s), the height of the curve at the point where the slope is s.
  • Faint dashed traces: the previous setting of a or f0, kept for comparison.
  • Readouts: x, s, f, g, h and dg/ds.
See itShow the tangent at your current settings, with the Readouts panel open. Watch for: the blue dot on the vertical axis at the height of g, and the readouts for x, s, f, g, h and dg/ds.

Fixed: k = 1/2, so f(x) = ½k(x − a)² + f0 = ¼(x − a)² + f0. All quantities are pure numbers, with no units.

03

The intercept g labels each point by its slope

The slope s = df/dx = k(x − a) increases steadily, so each slope belongs to exactly one point of the curve (notes, 3.4). A point of the tangent at horizontal position X stands at height f + s(X − x). Putting X = 0 gives the intercept on the vertical axis, g = f − sx (notes, 3.5), the blue dot in the sim.

Notes (3.4) and (3.5); x is the point where the slope is s, and k = 1/2 here.

At the opening setting, x = 2.00, a = 0 and f0 = 0.50, the slope is s = 1.00, the height is f = 1.50 and the intercept is g = −0.50. With a = 0 and f0 = 0.50, g = 0.50 − ¼x². From x = 0 to x = 3 it falls from 0.50 to −1.75, crossing zero near x = √2 ≈ 1.41, while f itself rises to 2.75.

See itSet a = 0 and f0 = 0.50, then sweep x from −1.50 to 3.00. Watch for: the blue dot on the vertical axis moving as x grows, and the g readout ending at −1.75 when x reaches 3.00.
04

The blue trace has slope −x

Changing the slope by ds changes f by s dx and the product sx by s dx + x ds. The s dx terms cancel, so dg = −x ds (notes, 3.7). The differential of g has ds and no dx, so g is a function of the slope alone, and the point comes back as x = −dg/ds (3.8).

Notes (3.7) and (3.8): the slope of the blue trace is the tangent point with its sign reversed.

The readout dg/ds is measured from neighbouring values of g and s at x ± 0.001, not from this formula, and it agrees with it. At x = 2.00 it reads −2.00, at x = 1.00 it reads −1.00 and at x = −1.00 it reads +1.00, whatever a and f0 are.

See itSet x = 2.00, keeping your a and f0. Watch for: the dg/ds readout at −2.00, the tangent point with its sign reversed.
See itMove the tangent point to x = −1.00. Watch for: the dg/ds readout at +1.00, now positive because x is negative.
05

A sideways shift moves g and leaves h alone

The height at slope s is the height of the curve at the point where the slope is s. On this curve it contains no a, while the intercept does.

The two labels of the curve, with k = 1/2 as in the sim.
At s = 1 the height is h = 1.50 for both a = 0 and a = 1. The intercept is g = −0.50 at a = 0 and −1.50 at a = 1.

Move a from 0 to 1 and look at the slope s = 1.00. The tangent with that slope now touches at x = 3, and it crosses the vertical axis lower by a·s = 1, so g falls from −0.50 to −1.50, while h stays 1.50. A vertical shift is different: raising f0 from 0.50 to 1.00 at x = 2 lifts h from 1.50 to 2.00 and g from −0.50 to 0.00.

See itSweep x at a = 0, then move to a = 1 and sweep again, with f0 = 0.50. Watch for: the orange trace lying on its dashed copy while the blue trace has moved, with h = 1.50 and g = −1.50 at s = 1.00.
See itSweep x at f0 = 0.50, then raise f0 to 1.00 and set x = 2.00, with a = 0. Watch for: both traces lifted above their dashed copies, with h = 2.00 and g = 0.00 at x = 2.00.
06

The tangents alone rebuild the curve

A pair (s, g) fixes one tangent line completely, Y = g + sX. Give the intercept for every slope and you have given the whole family of tangents, and the curve is their envelope (notes, after 3.8). Then x = −dg/ds returns each tangent point, and f = g + sx returns its height.

Ten of the lines Y = g + sX for a = 1 and f0 = 0.50. They outline the dotted curve, lowest at x = 1, height 0.50.

This is why g keeps the position of the curve and h does not: h(s) is the same for a = −1 and a = 1, so it cannot say where the curve was. With Rebuild from tangents on, the sim hides the curve and draws 31 lines from the blue trace alone. For a = 1 and f0 = 0.50 they outline a curve with its lowest point at x = 1.0, height 0.50.

See itSweep x at a = 1 and f0 = 0.50, then turn Rebuild from tangents on. Watch for: the curve gone, and a family of straight lines outlining a curve with its lowest point at x = 1.0, height 0.50.
07

Where it matters

  • Helmholtz function. The slope of U(S, V) with respect to S is T. Exchanging S for T gives F = U − TS (notes, 3.11), and dF = −S dT − p dV (3.13) gives S back as −(∂F/∂T)V, the thermodynamic copy of x = −dg/ds.
  • Enthalpy and Gibbs. The same exchange in V, where the slope is −p, gives H = U + pV. Doing both exchanges gives G = U − TS + pV.
  • Why bother. A laboratory controls T and p, not S, and the transform changes variables without losing the information in U(S, V) (notes, Section 3.1).
The same exchange as g = f − sx, with f = U, x = S and s = T, at fixed V.
Go deeper: the sign convention

In mechanics the transform from the Lagrangian to the Hamiltonian uses the opposite sign. The sim, like the thermodynamic notes, uses g = f − sx. The transform needs the slope to increase steadily, so that each slope belongs to one point; this parabola does.

08

Summary

In one line. The sim draws a parabola with a movable tangent, and traces beside it two quantities that depend on the slope s of that tangent: the intercept g (blue) and the height h (orange).

Key points

  • g = f − sx labels the point by its slope, and dg/ds = −x.
  • g carries the position of the curve; h(s) does not.
  • Tangents drawn from g(s) outline the curve.

Common mix-ups

  • “The intercept follows the height of the curve.” At a = 0, f rises to 2.75 at x = 3, but sx grows twice as fast, so g falls to −1.75.
  • “dg/ds is the slope s of the tangent.” At x = 2 the slope is +1.00 and the blue trace slopes at −2.00. dg/ds = −x.
  • “A sideways shift moves both traces.” h(s) has no a in it. Only g moves.

Things to try on your own

  • With a = 0 and f0 = 0.50, find the x where g crosses zero, and compare it with √2.
  • Find x where s = 1 for a = −1 and for a = 1, and compare h and g.
  • Sweep x at a = −1 and f0 = 1.00, turn Rebuild on, and read the lowest point of the outlined curve.
